summary: Western Afghanistan (Herat, Sistan) and the north (Balkh/Tokharistan) were taken into the Rashidun and Umayyad caliphates in the 650s-710s and governed by caliphal governors. The east and south-east (Kabul, Zabulistan, Ghazni) resisted for two centuries under the Turk/Hindu Shahis and the Zunbils, paying tribute at times, and came under lasting Muslim rule only with the Saffarids (870) and Ghaznavids (late 10th c.), who recognised the Abbasid caliph. Ghor was Islamised only in the 11th century and later ruled by the Abbasid-recognising Ghurids. Nuristan (Kafiristan) was never ruled by a caliphate or recognising dynasty; it was conquered and converted by Amir Abdur Rahman Khan in 1895-96.

units.label: Herat and Badghis (Harat, Badghis)

caliphate.who: Rashidun, Umayyad and Abbasid governors of Khurasan; later Tahirids, Samanids, Ghaznavids, Seljuks, Ghurids (all recognising the Abbasids)
caliphate.dates: c. 652 treaty; Arab governor appointed; caliphal rule continuous through Abbasid era; recognising dynasties to 1215

units.notes: Ruled directly: the local ruler made a peace treaty covering Herat, Badghis and Pushang at the first conquest (c. 652) and an Arab governor was installed. Badghis's Hephthalite prince Nizak surrendered to Qutayba in 705 and revolted in 709; after that the area was firmly part of Umayyad Khurasan.
units.uncertain: Exact year of first conquest of Herat varies in sources (643 vs 652); I did not open the Iranica 'Herat iii' medieval article (URL not found).

units.label: Sīstān (Zaranj) and Farah

caliphate.who: Rashidun (under Uthman), Umayyad and Abbasid governors of Sijistan; then Saffarids (recognised by the caliph as governors for a time), Samanid-vassal Saffarids, Ghaznavids
caliphate.dates: Zarang surrendered 31/652 (raids from 643-644); caliphal governors to 861; Saffarids 861-1003; Ghaznavid 1003 on

units.notes: Ruled directly: Zarang surrendered peacefully in 652 and became the Arab base for raids east against the Zunbils and Kabul Shahs. Sistan was a Kharijite stronghold, but still a caliphal province, until Ya'qub b. al-Layth rose there (861). Farah sits on the Zarang-Herat road and shared this history.
units.uncertain: Farah is grouped with Sistan by geography; I did not open a source about Farah specifically.

units.label: Balkh and Lower Ṭukhāristān

caliphate.who: Umayyad governors of Khurasan (Qutayba b. Muslim, Asad b. Abd Allah); Abbasid governors; then Tahirids, Samanids, Ghaznavids, Seljuks, Ghurids (recognising the Abbasids)
caliphate.dates: Tribute only 652-c.705; firm control from 705 (Qutayba) and 709-710 (after Nizak's revolt); Balkh briefly capital of Khurasan from 725; to 1220

units.notes: First submissions in 651-652 were tribute agreements that local princes broke. From Qutayba's campaigns (705-710) Arab district officers were placed beside the local princes, and in 725 Governor Asad rebuilt Balkh and moved the Khurasan capital there. So this was directly ruled, not only tributary.
units.uncertain: Kunduz/Baghlan/Takhar (old Tokharistan, Khulm, Andarab) are grouped with Balkh by region; I did not open separate sources on each. Exact date of first Arab entry to Balkh is given as 652 or 653.

units.label: Gūzgān (Juzjan) and Fāryāb

caliphate.who: Umayyad governors of Khurasan after 709; Abbasid governors; then local Farighunid amirs as vassals of the Saffarids, Samanids and Ghaznavids
caliphate.dates: c. 709-710 (Nizak's revolt in Guzgan suppressed) to 1010; recognising dynasties to 1215

islamic_states.name: Farighunids (vassals of Saffarid Amr, then Samanids, then Ghaznavids)
Durrani / Barakzai Afghanistan
islamic_states.dates: 18th c. onwards (Uzbek khanates of Maymana etc. absorbed in the 19th c.)

units.notes: Guzgan was part of lower Tokharistan, where Nizak raised a revolt in 709 that Qutayba put down; after that the area was within Umayyad Khurasan. In the 9th-10th centuries it was held by the local Muslim Farighunids as Samanid and then Ghaznavid vassals.
units.uncertain: Neither source I opened gives a firm date for the Arab conquest of Guzgan itself or says whether the Farighunids named the caliph on their coins. Sar-i Pul and Faryab are grouped here by region.

units.label: Badakhshān

caliphate.who: Samanids (coins at the Badakhshan mint name the Abbasid caliphs al-Radi, al-Muti', al-Ta'i), then Ghaznavids
caliphate.dates: Samanid governors c. 920-990s; Ghaznavid from late 10th c.; earlier 8th-c. Arab presence (tribute) not dated precisely

islamic_states.name: Samanids (governors such as al-Harith b. Harb)
Durrani / Barakzai Afghanistan
islamic_states.dates: Durrani invasion mid-18th c.; tributary to Kabul by 1859; autonomy ended 1881

units.notes: As part of Tokharistan, Badakhshan was likely tributary to the Umayyads at first. Firm evidence of rule comes from 10th-century Samanid coins struck in Badakhshan with the Abbasid caliph's name. Ismaili Islam was spread there by Nasir Khusraw in the 11th century, and later it was usually run by semi-autonomous local mirs.
units.uncertain: I could not open an Iranica history section for Badakhshan (only geography/name sections exist). No source I opened dates the first Arab conquest. The coin study's date for the Ghaznavid takeover (it says 984, under 'Mahmud') does not match Mahmud's reign and is not used.

units.label: Kābulistān (Kabul, Kāpisā)

caliphate.who: Saffarids (870, Ya'qub b. al-Layth, recognised by the caliph as governor), then Ghaznavids (recognised the Abbasids; Mahmud invested 999), Ghurids
caliphate.dates: Saffarid 870 (perhaps lost c. 878); Ghaznavid from 977 to the 1150s; Ghurid to c. 1215

units.notes: Before 870 this land was not ruled by the caliphate: Arab raids (Abd al-Rahman b. Samura took Kabul c. 664 but left) were temporary, and the Turk Shahi kings paid tribute at times (submission to al-Mahdi 775-785; defeat by al-Ma'mun's forces 814/815 with forced conversion and tribute). Lasting Muslim rule began with the Saffarid conquest of 870 and firmly with the Ghaznavids from 977.
units.uncertain: Sources disagree on whether the Hindu Shahis retook Kabul after 878 and held it until Sabuktigin (977); 'History of Kabul' presents 870 as the lasting start. Parwan and Wardak are grouped here by region (Wardak is also partly Hazarajat).

units.label: Lamghān and Nagarahāra (Jalalabad)

caliphate.who: Ghaznavids (recognised the Abbasid caliph)
caliphate.dates: Fought over 986-991; firmly Ghaznavid after Jayapala's defeat at Peshawar, 1001; Ghurid in the late 12th c.

units.notes: This was Hindu Shahi land (Kabul Shahi tribute periods apply). Sabuktigin plundered Lamghan after Jayapala broke a treaty (c. 986-988) and routed him in 991. After Mahmud's victory at Peshawar in 1001, all Shahi territory west of the Indus submitted to the Ghaznavids.
units.uncertain: No source I opened gives an exact annexation year for Laghman/Nangarhar specifically. Upper Laghman (Alingar/Alishang) bordered Kafiristan and stayed non-Muslim until the 1890s.

units.label: Kunar valley (Chaghan-Sarai)

caliphate.who: No caliphate or recognising dynasty confirmed as ruling the valley

units.notes: The lower valley had a Muslim town (Chaghan-Sarai) by Babur's time, whose people mixed with Kafir customs. Much of the province was part of the Kafiristan borderland, and its non-Muslim parts were conquered and converted under Abdur Rahman Khan in the 1890s.
units.uncertain: The Wikipedia province article's claim of 'Gabari sultans' ruling 900-1190 is poorly sourced and is not used. I could not confirm whether the Ghaznavids held the lower valley; if they did, the category would be caliphate_ruled.

units.label: Kāfiristān (Nuristan)

caliphate.who: Never ruled by a caliphate or recognising dynasty

islamic_states.name: Barakzai Emirate of Afghanistan (Amir Abdur Rahman Khan)

units.notes: Politically independent and non-Muslim until Abdur Rahman Khan's columns took it in about 40 days in winter 1895-96, followed by forced conversion. Earlier contact was raids only, e.g. a possible raid by Mahmud of Ghazni on 'Nardain'. Surrounding Muslim states never ruled it.
units.uncertain: Whether any earlier raid (Mahmud c. 1020; Timur 1398, often mentioned elsewhere) actually reached Nuristan; I did not open a source on Timur's raid.

units.label: Ghazna

caliphate.who: Saffarids (Lawik rulers reduced to tributaries), then Ghaznavids (recognised the Abbasids), Ghurids
caliphate.dates: Saffarid conquest c. 870; Lawik tributary 877; Ghaznavid 962/977 - 1163; Ghurid 1173 - c. 1215

units.notes: An Arab raid reached the area in 683, and in 769 Ma'n b. Za'ida defeated the Zunbils near Ghazni and took tribute; both were temporary or tributary. Lasting Muslim rule came with Ya'qub b. al-Layth (c. 870) and above all Alptigin's capture in 962, after which Ghazni was the Ghaznavid capital (977-1163).
units.uncertain: Whether the Lawik rulers were Muslim is disputed in the sources.

caliphate.who: Saffarids (Lawik ruler of Gardez made tributary 877), then Ghaznavids and Ghurids (recognised the Abbasids)

units.notes: Gardez (Paktya) is the best documented: Ya'qub b. al-Layth made its Lawik ruler a tributary in 877, and it then lay inside the Ghaznavid heartland next to Ghazni. Logar lies between Kabul and Gardez. Khost and Paktika were tribal uplands where state control was probably light.
units.uncertain: No source I opened documents administration of Khost or Paktika specifically; grouped here by geography. If treated strictly, Khost/Paktika might only reach islamic_state_ruled.

units.label: Zābulistān, Zamindāwar, Bust and Rukhkhaj (Kandahar)

caliphate.who: Saffarids (Ya'qub, recognised by the caliph as governor of Sistan), then Ghaznavids and Ghurids (recognised the Abbasids). Earlier: Rashidun/Umayyad conquest of Bust and tribute from the Zunbils.
caliphate.dates: Bust and Zabul treaty 656; Zunbil tribute intermittently 7th-8th c.; Saffarid conquest 870; Ghaznavid c. 977 - 1150s; Ghurid to c. 1215

islamic_states.name: Arghuns; Mughals and Safavids contesting Kandahar

units.notes: Mixed in the first two centuries: Bost and Zabul submitted by treaty in 656 and Arab expeditions came from Sistan (e.g. Abbad b. Ziyad, 673-681). But the Zunbils held Zamindawar and Zabulistan, defeated an Umayyad army in 698, and paid tribute only at times (698/711/769; nominal submission to al-Mahdi). Lasting Muslim rule came when Ya'qub b. al-Layth destroyed the Zunbils in 870.
units.uncertain: I could not open the Iranica 'Bost' history text, so I could not confirm whether Bust itself was a continuous Arab garrison under the Umayyads/Abbasids (if yes, status for Bust would be 'direct'). Last Zunbil killed 865 vs 870 in different sources.

caliphate.who: Saffarids, Samanids, Ghaznavids, Ghurids (recognising the Abbasids) claimed the Hazarajat region

units.notes: Mountain land between Ghor, Ghazni and Kandahar. General sources list it in the Saffarid-to-Ghurid realms, but the Hazarajat was in practice autonomous under local chiefs until Abdur Rahman Khan's conquest in the 1880s-90s. Caliphal-era rule here is therefore likely nominal.

units.label: Bāmiyān

caliphate.who: Saffarids (870), Samanids, Ghaznavids, then the Ghurid branch of Bamiyan (Ghurids recognised the Abbasids). Earlier: the Sher of Bamiyan submitted/converted under the Abbasids.
caliphate.dates: Sher's conversion late 8th c.; Saffarid 870; Ghaznavid 11th c.; Ghurid branch 1155-1212

units.notes: In the 8th century a tributary local kingdom whose ruler (the Sher) converted, per al-Ya'qubi as reported in a modern source. It came under Saffarid control in 870 and Ghaznavid rule in the 11th century. From 1155 to 1212 it was the capital of a Ghurid branch kingdom stretching to the Oxus.
units.uncertain: Sources conflict on when Bamiyan was Islamised (late 8th c. Sher conversion vs 'under Sultan Mahmud'). Iranica's history article on Bamiyan could not be opened.

caliphate.who: Ghaznavids (loose vassalage from 1011), then the Ghurid sultans, who kept close relations with the Abbasids (embassies; Ghiyath al-Din admitted to al-Nasir's futuwwa order)

islamic_states.name: Kartids, Timurids, Safavids/Mughals (fringes), Durrani/Barakzai
islamic_states.dates: 13th c. onwards; interior largely autonomous until the 1890s

units.notes: Arabs never set up lasting control here. Ghor was Islamised late, through Ghaznavid campaigns of Mahmud and Mas'ud in the early 11th century that left it in loose vassalage. Its own Ghurid dynasty then built an empire and maintained relations with the Abbasid caliph. Juzjani's story that an early Ghurid prince was legitimised by Harun al-Rashid is a legend, not proof of caliphal rule.
units.uncertain: Whether 'cordial relations / embassies / futuwwa' amounts to formal investiture; khutba and coin evidence was not checked directly.

summary: Sind and Multan were conquered by the Umayyads in 711-713 and governed by caliphal governors, then by local dynasties that read the khutba for the Abbasids (Habbarids of Mansura, Banu Munabbih of Multan) or, at Multan, the Fatimids. Makran was entered under Umar (644) and was the launching base for 711. Northern Punjab, the Peshawar valley and Islamabad's area stayed under the Hindu Shahis until the Ghaznavid conquest (1001-1026), and the Ghaznavids recognised the Abbasid caliph. Gilgit-Baltistan and Azad Kashmir were never under a caliphate; they came under local Muslim dynasties, the Kashmir Sultanate and the Mughals from the 14th-16th centuries, then Sikh and Dogra (non-Muslim) rule from 1819-1840 until 1947.

units.label: Sind (Mansūra, Daybul)

caliphate.who: Umayyad governors (Muhammad b. al-Qasim 711-715, Junayd, al-Hakam b. Awana) and Abbasid governors; then the Habbarids of Mansura, who read the Friday prayer in the Abbasid caliph's name

islamic_states.dates: 11th - 14th c.; Iltutmish took Sind 1228, invested by the Abbasid caliph 1229

units.notes: Ruled directly: Muhammad b. al-Qasim took Debal, Nirun, Sehwan, Brahmanabad and Aror in 711-713, and Sind became a caliphal province with garrison cities (al-Mahfuza, al-Mansura). After 861 the Habbarids ruled independently but kept the khutba for the Abbasids until Mahmud of Ghazni destroyed Mansura in 1026.
units.uncertain: The Soomra and Samma dynasties' relation to any caliph was not checked. Classical narrative (Chachnama, al-Baladhuri) was not consulted directly.

units.label: Punjab: Multan (Mūltān) and Lahore

caliphate.who: Multan: Umayyad direct (713), Banu Munabbih (recognised Abbasids), Ismaili rulers reading the khutba for the Fatimid caliph. Rest of Punjab (Lahore, Salt Range): Ghaznavids (recognised Abbasids), Ghurids, Delhi Sultanate (invested by the Abbasid caliph 1229).
caliphate.dates: Multan 713 - 1010; Lahore and central/northern Punjab c. 1014-1021 onward

units.notes: Southern Punjab (Multan) was ruled directly by the Umayyads from 713 and then by recognising local amirs; the Fatimid khutba period also counts. Central and northern Punjab belonged to the Hindu Shahis until Mahmud's victories (Chach 1008, Nandana 1014) and annexation around 1021. From then on it was ruled by Abbasid-recognising dynasties. Sikh rule (1799-1849) was a non-Islamic interlude before the British.
units.uncertain: Exact annexation year of Lahore (1021 vs later) varies; eastern Punjab districts' timing not checked individually.

units.label: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa: Peshawar valley (Purushapura), Swat, Hazara, Chitral

units.notes: The Peshawar valley was Hindu Shahi territory until Mahmud's victory at Peshawar on 27 November 1001; afterwards it was ruled by Abbasid-recognising dynasties. Exceptions: the high valleys of Chitral (Kalasha still non-Muslim today), upper Swat/Dir and Kohistan were not effectively governed by these dynasties and were Islamised later under local rulers. Sikh rule 1834-1849 was non-Islamic.
units.uncertain: Chitral, Dir, Swat and Kohistan were not researched individually. The Jayapala article gives 27 September 1001 for the Peshawar battle, the Hindu Shahis article 27 November 1001.

units.notes: Mostly self-governing Pashtun tribal land. Muslim states reached parts of it: Babur took Bajaur in 1518, and Kurram was taxed by Kabul with periodic expeditions and got a resident governor around 1848. British control under the Durand Line (1893) never fully pacified it.

units.label: Baluchistan: Makrān (Kech), Ṭurān (Quṣdār/Khuzdar), Kalat

caliphate.who: Makran: Rashidun entry (644) and Umayyad control (base for the 711 invasion; part of the caliphal province of Sind). Turan/Qusdar: via local Muslim rulers reading the khutba for the Abbasids (Mu'tazz at Kizkanan, mid-10th c.) and Habbarid Mansura reaching Khuzdar; later Saffarid and Ghaznavid tributaries.
caliphate.dates: Makran 644 / 711 onward; Turan mid-9th - 10th c.; Ghaznavid suzerainty 976-77 to 12th c.

islamic_states.name: Ma'danid rulers of Makran (tributary to Saffarids)
Ghaznavid suzerainty over Makran and Qusdar
Local Makran maliks; Safavid influence in west
Mughals and Safavids (Quetta/Shal as part of Kandahar)
Khanate of Kalat (Durrani suzerainty 1747 on; British from 1839/1876)

units.notes: Makran (coast and Kech) was entered under Umar (23/644) and served as the Umayyad route to Sind in 711, so it counts as directly ruled, though Umar barred further advance and control later loosened. Inner Baluchistan (Turan/Qusdar) is less clear: Iranica says it is not named in the early conquest accounts. Caliphal rule there is shown only through local rulers reading the Abbasid khutba in the 10th century, before it became a Ghaznavid tributary. The northern Pashtun belt (Quetta-Pishin, Zhob) and the Marri-Bugti hills followed Kandahar's or tribal history.
units.uncertain: Early Umayyad campaigns against Kikan/Qiqan and Qusdar (reported by al-Baladhuri) were not seen quoted in any source I opened. Wikipedia's 'Rashidun conquest of Turan c. 650' conflicts with Iranica and is treated as unreliable. Northern Baluchistan not researched separately.

caliphate.who: Never ruled by a caliphate or recognising dynasty

islamic_states.name: Kashmir Sultanate (Shihab-ud-Din's campaigns into Gilgit, Baltistan)
Maqpon rajas of Skardu (Muslim; Ali Sher Khan Anchan from 1580)

units.notes: Islam arrived through Sufi missionaries from Kashmir and Central Asia from the 14th century (Baltistan largely Nurbakhshi by the 17th century; Hunza Ismaili). It was then ruled by local Muslim dynasties, with brief Kashmir Sultanate campaigns and Mughal intervention. Muslim rule ended with the Sikh and Dogra conquests of 1839-1870, which lasted until the 1947 Gilgit revolt.
units.uncertain: How firm the Mughal hold over Baltistan was (Wikipedia speaks of 'conquest' 1586 and intrusions 1634-36); the date the Gilgit Trakhans became Muslim; whether Durrani suzerainty reached the area.

units.label: Azad Kashmir (Muzaffarabad, Poonch, Mirpur, Bhimber)

Mughals (Kashmir Subah; Gakhar and Bomba chiefs as local rulers)

units.notes: Never under a caliphate or a recognising dynasty. Muslim rule came with the Kashmir Sultanate (from 1339) and especially the Mughals, under whom local Muslim chiefs founded Mirpur (c. 1640) and Muzaffarabad (1646). Afghan (Durrani) rule followed until the Sikh conquest of 1819 and Dogra rule (1846-1947).
units.uncertain: I did not confirm that the Kashmir Sultanate governed the Muzaffarabad/Poonch/Mirpur hills (vs only the Valley); the Mughal date (1586) is for Kashmir as a whole. Whether Ghaznavid campaigns ever held Mirpur/Bhimber was not checked (no source I opened says so).
